# How to Write Art Style Prompts That Actually Work (With Copy-Paste Examples)

> **In short:** An art style prompt is a short text instruction that tells an AI image tool to redraw a photo in the look of a chosen style — a 16-bit video game, a watercolor, a 90s cartoon. The recipe is the same in every tool: subject, style, mood, technical detail. Below are six copy-paste patterns you can try today.

You took a great photo of your dog at the park last weekend. It's nice. The kind of nice that sits in your camera roll for three months. What if the same photo could come out looking like a Saturday morning cartoon, a worn paperback cover, or a Studio Ghibli frame? That is what an art style prompt does, and writing one is simpler than you might think.

## Before you start

You need an AI image tool that takes both a reference photo and a text prompt. Common choices are Midjourney, DALL-E (inside ChatGPT), Stable Diffusion, and Adobe Firefly. The menus differ, but the prompt logic below works in all of them. A free tier is enough to experiment.

## Step 1 — Name the subject in plain words

Every good prompt starts with what is actually in the picture. Skip the poetry. Skip the clever phrasing. Just say what is there, in the simplest possible way. The AI does not reward fancy vocabulary — it rewards clear vocabulary.

💬 Example:
`A golden retriever sitting on green grass, sunny afternoon`

You'll know it worked when the first result clearly shows your subject, not a different dog, not a generic animal, not a cat.

## Step 2 — Pick one art style and name it

This is where the visual change happens. The more specific the style, the more consistent the result. "Painting" alone is too vague. "Oil painting in the style of Van Gogh's later period" is much better. Choose one style per prompt. Mixing two usually muddles both.

A few directions to try:
- 16-bit pixel art (think SNES-era video game)
- Watercolor with soft edges
- Studio Ghibli anime style
- Vintage 1970s film photograph
- Oil painting with thick brushstrokes
- Pencil sketch with crosshatching
- Risograph print, limited color palette
- Claymation / plasticine look

💬 Example:
`A golden retriever sitting on green grass, sunny afternoon, painted in 16-bit pixel art style, SNES color palette`

You'll know it worked when the image clearly shows that style's visual fingerprint — chunky pixels, soft watercolor bleeds, or visible brushstrokes that match what you asked for.

## Step 3 — Add a mood or atmosphere word

Two prompts with the same subject and style can look completely different because of one word. Words like `moody`, `cheerful`, `dreamy`, `gritty`, `nostalgic`, and `ethereal` shift colors, lighting, and facial expressions all at once. Treat this as the emotional seasoning.

💬 Example:
`A golden retriever sitting on green grass, sunny afternoon, painted in 16-bit pixel art style, SNES color palette, moody and nostalgic`

You'll know it worked when the colors and lighting feel like the mood you asked for — dim and moody, or warm and bright, never in between.

## Step 4 — Add one or two technical details

Technical words describe the camera, the lens, the light, and the framing. They sharpen the result and make it feel intentional rather than random. Pick one or two — more than that and the prompt starts fighting itself.

Useful technical words:
- `shallow depth of field` (blurry background)
- `golden hour lighting` (warm sunset light)
- `low angle shot` (looking up at the subject)
- `centered composition`
- `soft focus` or `sharp focus`
- `cinematic aspect ratio`

💬 Example:
`A golden retriever sitting on green grass, sunny afternoon, painted in 16-bit pixel art style, SNES color palette, moody and nostalgic, shallow depth of field, golden hour lighting`

You'll know it worked when the composition and lighting match what you described — the background blurs out, the warm light comes in from the side, the subject is clearly the focus.

## Step 5 — Combine the four parts in one line

The full prompt structure is:

`[subject], [style], [mood], [technical detail]`

A finished prompt for the dog photo might read like this:

`A golden retriever sitting on green grass at sunset, Studio Ghibli anime style, soft watercolor textures, peaceful and warm, soft focus, golden hour lighting`

One sentence. Paste it into Midjourney, DALL-E, or Stable Diffusion and you get a real image. You'll know it worked when the four pieces feel coherent — the style, mood, and lighting all agree with each other instead of pulling in opposite directions.

## Step 6 — Change one thing at a time when you iterate

The first result is rarely the best one. The trick is to never rewrite the whole prompt. Swap one ingredient and see what happens. Change `Studio Ghibli` to `Makoto Shinkai`. Change `peaceful and warm` to `dreamy and melancholic`. Change `golden hour` to `overcast morning`. That way, when something goes wrong, you know exactly which piece caused it.

You'll know it worked when you can say, in plain words, why you like or dislike each new version. That sentence is the actual skill you're building.

## Common mistakes

- **Stacking too many styles in one prompt.** `Watercolor, oil painting, pixel art, anime` confuses the AI. Pick one, run it, then try a different one.
- **Vague style words.** `Cool`, `artistic`, `beautiful` mean different things to different people — and to the AI. Use a named style with a clear visual identity.
- **Forgetting the subject.** A style alone (`a watercolor painting, soft and dreamy`) gives you a generic image with no anchor. Always start with what is actually in your photo.
- **Skipping iteration.** One shot rarely nails it. Plan for five or six versions before you judge a prompt.
- **Ignoring image quality words.** Adding `highly detailed`, `8k`, or `masterpiece` can over-polish the result and wash out the style. Test with and without.

## What this means for you

- **If you post on social media for fun**: A stylized version of an ordinary photo — your lunch, your morning walk, your cat — gets more attention than another filter. Try one prompt on a photo you already have today.
- **If you are building a creative habit**: Pick one style a week and run the same photo through it. By the end of the month you will have a small visual library, and you will start to feel how each style reacts to the same subject.
- **If you want to use this for work or side projects**: Save the prompts that worked. Build a personal library of 10-15 styles you can mix and match. This becomes a real asset for newsletters, blog headers, or product mockups.

## Wrap-up

Art style prompts are not magic. They are a small recipe. Subject, style, mood, technical detail. Once you have the four parts, the same recipe works on any photo, in any tool. Try one prompt today: pick a photo you already like, choose a single style that excites you, paste the template from Step 5 into your tool of choice. Five minutes, one sentence, one new image. That is the whole game.
